hooks.text: A postage stamp declaring Pluto unexplored inspired a spacecraft to visit it.
Why did a tiny postage stamp taunt NASA into visiting Pluto?
One postage stamp traveled 3 billion miles to answer a 1991 insult.

title: The Stamp That Sent a Probe to Pluto
description: How a defiant United States postage stamp inspired NASA's New Horizons mission to fly past Pluto.

beats.text: A postage stamp declaring Pluto unexplored inspired a spacecraft to visit it.
beats.visual: USPS Pluto Not Yet Explored stamp, 1991

beats.text: In 1991, the postal service released stamps showing every planet alongside its visitor except the ninth.
beats.visual: 1991 planetary exploration postage stamp set by USPS

beats.text: The Pluto stamp simply read, Pluto: Not Yet Explored.
beats.visual: Close-up of the 1991 Pluto Not Yet Explored stamp
queries: Pluto Not Yet Explored stamp close up

beats.text: The phrase irked scientists so much it became a call to arms for a new mission.
beats.visual: Principal Investigator Alan Stern at a press conference, 2006

beats.text: On January 19, 2006, New Horizons launched as the fastest object ever sent from Earth.
beats.visual: Launch of the New Horizons spacecraft on an Atlas V rocket, 2006

beats.text: A Jupiter gravity assist shaved three years off the voyage, sending the probe speeding toward the outer solar system.
beats.visual: Jupiter as photographed by the New Horizons spacecraft, 2007

beats.text: On July 14, 2015, the spacecraft finally completed its historic close flyby of Pluto.
beats.visual: High-resolution color view of Pluto's surface captured by New Horizons, 2015

beats.text: Hidden onboard was that exact 1991 stamp, finally delivered to its destination.
beats.visual: Artist concept of the New Horizons spacecraft at Pluto, 2015
